attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the mechanism (data centers) and his phrase 'too much speculation'. No conditions or horizon to keep. Causal is a fair kind.

contract.note: Reading 'too much speculation' as building beyond credible demand is an ordinary reading, but the speaker gave no benchmark. Requiring both environmental risk and overbuilding is fair to his sentence.

evidence.note: Mistral reporting on its own model's footprint. It shows generative AI has environmental burdens, but it covers one model's lifecycle, not data-center construction or speculation.
Shows duplicated grid requests and upward-biased demand forecasts. These are proposals, not built capacity, so it does not show overbuilding.
Low vacancy and high preleasing point against broad overbuilding, but the data mixes cloud and AI demand and leases are not utilization.
Links current data-center construction to water stress and modeled emissions growth. Supports the environmental-threat part only.

reviews.rationale: Some evidence links AI data-center buildout to environmental risk (e4, with e1 as context). Nothing in the packet shows that built generative-AI capacity exceeded real demand: e2 covers requests only, and e3 points somewhat the other way without isolating generative AI. The support condition needs both parts, and the contradiction condition is not met, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus reports the study's finding and adds his own judgement that the figure is a massive overestimate.

semantics.note: Keeps his 'human tasks' wording, the 2.5% figure, and the physical-labor exclusion. The study actually measured complete remote freelance projects done by agents, which is narrower than 'human tasks'.

contract.note: Splits the claim into the study's figure and exclusion, which can be checked, and the size of the overestimate, which he gave no threshold for. That split is fair.

evidence.note: The original announcement reports a 2.5% top automation rate, measured on freelance projects rather than all human tasks.
The paper's sourcing criteria confirm that physical-labor projects were excluded. It gives no weighted estimate across all human work.

reviews.rationale: What holds: the study did report a 2.5% maximum and did exclude physical labor. The '2.5% of human tasks' wording overstates the scope, since the unit was remote freelance projects. What is not established: no evidence measures how much including physical work would change the figure, so 'massive overestimate' is unproven.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Accurately restates three ongoing limitations. No quantifier is added.

contract.note: Reading 'concept of reality' by behaviour is ordinary and fair. Treating the claim as recurring limitations, not universal failure, matches his words.

evidence.note: A February 2026 evaluation finds hallucination persists across frontier model configurations, including those using web search.
A February 2026 peer-reviewed survey reports persistent reasoning failures in simple scenarios, plus embodied and physical reasoning failures.
A 2023 study of internal world representations. It is from a different period and answers the literal reading, not dependable real-world reasoning.

reviews.rationale: Studies from the target period (e1, e2) document ongoing hallucination, simple reasoning failures, and failures on real-world physical constraints in capable LLMs. e3 does not show these limitations were solved. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'There is just no way' is a firm impossibility claim with no deadline. Tying 'those expectations' to the AGI-level selling in the previous sentence is faithful.

contract.note: The early-resolution rule needs either verified delivery of AGI-level promises or an impossibility result. Both fit an unbounded impossibility claim, though what counts as AGI-level is the evaluator's reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own September 2026 announcement of benchmark gains. It is a company claim and does not independently verify AGI-level capability.
The benchmark's authors call Astra meaningful progress but explicitly say it is not AGI. The early-resolution rule is not met.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was given. Neither early-resolution event appears in the packet: Astra's gains are not independently verified as AGI-level (the ARC Prize authors say they are not), and no impossibility result exists. The claim stays unresolved.
